content: Propofol has been increasingly recognized as both effective and safe for procedural sedation (PS) in emergency department (ED) settings. However, its use is complicated by a narrow therapeutic window and the absence of a reversal agent. This review aimed to consolidate evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of propofol for PS in the ED. The objective of the review was to identify and evaluate all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared propofol to alternative sedative agents, including benzodiazepines, barbiturates, etomidate, and ketamine, in the ED setting. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering publications up to September 2013, with an additional search in February 2015. No language restrictions were applied. Reference lists of trials were reviewed, and trial authors were contacted for further information. The review included RCTs involving participants of all ages. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the quality of the included trials using The Cochrane Collaboration's risk of bias tool. Effect sizes were measured using mean difference (MD), odds ratio (OR), and 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 10 studies, involving 813 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Two studies included participants aged 18 years or younger, six studies included participants aged 18 years or older, one study included participants aged 16 to 65 years, and one study included adults without specifying the age range. Eight of the studies were found to have a high risk of bias, and the included studies were clinically heterogeneous, precluding meta-analysis. The primary outcomes of the review were adverse effects and participant satisfaction, as defined by the study authors. In one study comparing propofol/fentanyl with ketamine/midazolam, delayed adverse reactions such as nightmares and behavioral changes were observed in 10% of the ketamine/midazolam group but not in the propofol/fentanyl group. Seven studies reported no significant differences in adverse effects between intravenous propofol (with or without adjunctive analgesic agents) and alternative interventions. Three studies found no significant differences in pain at the injection site between propofol and other sedatives. Four studies reported no significant differences in participant satisfaction between propofol (with or without adjunctive analgesic agents) and alternative interventions, such as ketamine, etomidate, and midazolam. All studies used propofol without adjunctive analgesics, and most were small, with fewer than 100 participants. The quality of evidence for adverse effects and participant satisfaction was rated as very low. Nine studies reported secondary outcomes, excluding mortality, but the results could not be pooled due to differences in comparator interventions and reporting methods. Seven studies found no significant differences in the incidence of hypoxia between propofol (with or without adjunctive analgesics) and alternative interventions. The authors concluded that no definitive conclusions could be drawn regarding the comparative effects of intravenous propofol (with or without adjunctive analgesics) versus alternative sedatives for PS in the ED. This limitation was primarily due to the heterogeneity of comparator interventions, the small sample sizes in most studies, and the overall low quality of evidence.
